newsitem.title: IRAQ: Saddam's wounded son appears on TV, blames Iran.
newsitem.headline: Saddam's wounded son appears on TV, blames Iran.

text.p: Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday appeared on television on Tuesday for the first time since he was shot and appeared to blame neighbouring Iran for the attack on him five days ago.
Uday spoke at ease with a Qatari envoy and a reporter from the official Iraqi News Agency on Shebab television, Uday's private channel.

They were the first images of Uday since unidentified gunmen attacked him as he drove in the wealthy al-Mansour district of the Iraqi capital on Thursday. Several people, beside Uday, were reported to have been seriously wounded in the attack.
The pictures showed Uday looking relaxed with his body covered by a blanket and no bandages on his head. He did not move either hand to welcome the visitors.
Uday implicated Iran in the attack. "The treacherous people are known along with the place they come from....they tested us for eight years," he said in reference to the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war.
Uday was quoted by official media as describing the attack as "treachery" and said it was not a characteristic of Arabs.
Iraqi opposition groups abroad have claimed they were behind the attack.
Uday's brother Qusay, who heads Iraq's Special Security, accompanied Rashid al-Na'imi, who represented Sheikh Khalifa Bin Hamad al-Thani, head of Qatar's Cooperation Sports Club.
The bed at Ibn Sina Hospital in Baghdad was flanked with bouquets sent by diplomats, officials and heads of trades union.
"My father, may God preserve him...has said that I and Qusay are committed to martyrdom. This is nothing new to us," Uday told the INA reporter when asked to assure Iraqis of his safety.
The Qatari envoy described the attack on Uday as "a cowardly act."
"May God prolong your life. Everybody sends his greetings," he said.

He told Uday the Qatari government was ready to offer all medical services. "We are ready for everything ..anything ..everything will be ready for you in seconds...we wish that you will recover the soonest possible," he said.
Uday is chairman of Iraq's National Olympic Committee. He owns the newspaper Babel, Iraq's most influential, and runs the popular Shebab television channel.
"What I feel now from this condition is the same felt by a military commander dear to me being subjected to the same situation," he said.

Uday said he was thankful for thoughts expressed by Iraqis from all walks of life. "Through you I thank all the sons of our great people...They made us feel whatever we do to them they deserve more...God preserve Iraq and Saddam," he said.

Shebab television also showed festivities taking place in Baghdad to mark his safety. The spot where he was shot in the capital has turned into something like a shrine, frequented by thousands of Iraqis, slaughtering sheep and handing out sweets.
Several restaurants in Baghdad offered free meals and butchers in al-Mansour district were said to distribute meat free of charge in jubilation.
Iraq's Youth Federation, the largest state-run popular organisation, said on Tuesday it would hold large celebrations to mark Uday's survival.
